claims.text: Q235 steel in the as-received state has a typical population of non-metallic inclusions.
Pre-existing Mn-rich sulfide inclusions in Q235 steel act as local cathodic sites relative to the ferritic matrix.
Mn-rich sulfide inclusions enhance localized galvanic coupling with the ferritic matrix.
Inclusion-driven galvanic coupling accelerates localized corrosion in Q235 steel.
Reducing the relevant inclusions should suppress corrosion onset by limiting localized electrochemical reactions.
Refining or targeted heat treatment can reduce the concentration or modify the morphology of MnS and related oxide inclusions in Q235 steel.
Non-metallic oxide inclusions can also act as cathodic sites relative to the ferritic matrix.
Electrochemical-potential differences between inclusions and the surrounding iron matrix initiate localized galvanic cells.
These localized galvanic cells accelerate pit formation and corrosion.
Elevated temperature may enhance the kinetics of the proposed localized electrochemical reactions.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, inclusion-reduced samples will have lower pitting density under room-temperature and elevated-temperature corrosive conditions.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, inclusion-reduced samples will have lower corrosion-related weight loss.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, inclusion-reduced samples will exhibit more stable electrochemical impedance characteristics.
Untreated Q235 steel with standard inclusion content will exhibit more aggressive localized corrosion than inclusion-reduced material under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed inclusion mechanism is expected to be significant in chloride-containing environments and at elevated temperatures.
Other alloying elements or impurities could alter the measured corrosion response independently of the targeted inclusions.
Analogous observations in other alloy systems support a qualitative role for inclusions in promoting localized corrosion.
The cited Cr-Mn-Fe-Ni high-entropy-alloy study shows that Mn dissolution was associated with mass loss during exposure to molten FLiBe at 700 °C.

Failure of inclusion-modified specimens to show statistically significant improvements in weight loss, pitting density, and EIS at both tested temperatures would falsify the proposed inclusion-driven mechanism.
